questions.text: The tear film:
options: The mucin layer is in contact with the cornea
Is not important in the refraction of light entering the eye
originalOptions: The mucin layer is in contact with the cornea
Is not important in the refraction of light entering the eye
questions.correctAnswer: C) The mucin layer is in contact with the cornea
questions.correctAnswerText: The mucin layer is in contact with the cornea
questions.explanation: The tear film is trilaminar (lipid, aqueous, mucin), with the inner mucin layer directly wetting the hydrophobic corneal epithelium — making C correct and B wrong (three layers, not four). A is wrong because the tear film average thickness is only 3 µm (ranging from 2 to 5.5 µm), not 100 µm. D is wrong because the tear-air interface is actually a major refractive surface of the eye, so the tear film is optically important, not irrelevant.

questions.text: Aqueous humour is formed by:
questions.explanation: B and C are wrong because the iris and lens play no role in aqueous production — the iris only regulates pupil size, and the lens is purely refractive. D is a plausible-sounding distractor since the pars plana is part of the ciliary body region, but production occurs at the ciliary processes (pars plicata), not the pars plana. E is wrong because the trabecular meshwork is a drainage structure, not a secretory one.

questions.text: All of the following statements about the tear film are true EXCEPT:
options: Lysozyme and lactoferrin in the aqueous layer provide antibacterial protection
The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
The tear film keeps the corneal surface smooth, clear, and lubricated
Conjunctival goblet cells produce the inner mucin layer
The mucin layer allows the aqueous layer to wet the hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly
originalOptions: Lysozyme and lactoferrin in the aqueous layer provide antibacterial protection
The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
The tear film keeps the corneal surface smooth, clear, and lubricated
Conjunctival goblet cells produce the inner mucin layer
The mucin layer allows the aqueous layer to wet the hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly
questions.correctAnswer: B) The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
questions.correctAnswerText: The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
questions.explanation: The meibomian glands, located in the tarsal plates, secrete the outer lipid layer of the tear film, not the aqueous layer — the aqueous layer (about 90% of tear thickness) comes from the main and accessory lacrimal glands, and also carries antibacterial proteins like lysozyme and lactoferrin. A, C, D, and E are all correct descriptions of tear film anatomy.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer about the retina:
options: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the RPE
The RPE delivers vitamin K for rhodopsin production
originalOptions: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the RPE
The RPE delivers vitamin K for rhodopsin production
questions.correctAnswer: B) Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
questions.correctAnswerText: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
questions.explanation: The retinal ganglion cell axons converge at the optic disc and exit the eye as the optic nerve — this is why the optic disc, lacking photoreceptors, corresponds to the physiological blind spot. A is wrong because the retina has 10 histological layers, not 7. C is wrong on two counts: colour vision is mediated by cones (not rods), and there are three types of cones (not rods). D is wrong because the neurosensory retina is only loosely apposed to the RPE (not firmly attached) — this is exactly why retinal detachment can occur. E is wrong because the RPE recycles vitamin A (not vitamin K) for the visual cycle and rhodopsin regeneration.

questions.text: Most of the thickness of the cornea is formed by:
questions.explanation: The stroma (substantia propria) makes up about 90% of corneal thickness. It consists of organized collagen fibers that give the cornea its transparency and structural strength.

questions.text: Cornea is supplied by nerve fibers derived from:
questions.explanation: The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues in the body, supplied sensorially by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve — which is why corneal inflammation or ulceration is extremely painful.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a source of nutrients to the cornea?
questions.explanation: The cornea is avascular and is nourished by atmospheric oxygen, the aqueous humour, and the perilimbal capillary network. The vitreous humour is not a source of corneal nutrition.

questions.text: All of the following are avascular EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are vascular
originalOptions: All of the above are vascular
questions.explanation: The cornea and lens are explicitly avascular, nourished only by diffusion, and the vitreous is a clear gel with no vessels of its own. The sclera is a hypovascular collagenous coat. While it has a very limited internal blood supply, it is pierced by blood vessels and intimately connected to the overlying vascularised episclera, making it the only structure listed that is not completely avascular. Note: if option E had instead read "All of the above are avascular," E would be the more correct choice, since the sclera is technically hypovascular rather than completely avascular.

questions.text: All of the following are part of the uvea except:
questions.explanation: The uvea consists of the iris, ciliary body (which has two parts: pars plicata and pars plana), and the choroid. Schwalbe's line is an anatomical landmark at the anterior chamber angle (the termination of Descemet's membrane) and is not part of the uveal tract.

questions.text: The following is a part of uvea except:
questions.explanation: Bowman's membrane is a layer of the cornea and has no relation to the uveal tract.

questions.text: Optic disc diameter is:
questions.explanation: The optic disc diameter is used as a standard unit of measurement (Disc Diameter, DD) to describe the size and location of fundus lesions.

questions.text: Aqueous humor is secreted by:
questions.explanation: The ciliary processes are the precise anatomical site of aqueous humour secretion within the ciliary body.

questions.text: Corneal ulceration/anaesthesia is caused by injury to the ___ cranial nerve:
questions.explanation: Loss of corneal sensation (from trigeminal nerve injury) abolishes the protective blink reflex, leaving the cornea vulnerable to neurotrophic keratitis.

questions.text: Number of layers in the neurosensory retina is:
questions.explanation: The neurosensory retina classically consists of 9 layers, from the photoreceptors to the nerve fiber layer. The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is anatomically and functionally a separate, tenth layer.

questions.text: During accommodation for near vision, which of the following changes occurs?
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens
The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
The zonular fibres tighten and the lens flattens
The pupil dilates and the lens flattens
The cornea steepens while the lens remains unchanged
originalOptions: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens
The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
The zonular fibres tighten and the lens flattens
The pupil dilates and the lens flattens
The cornea steepens while the lens remains unchanged
questions.correctAnswer: B) The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
questions.correctAnswerText: The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
questions.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonular fibres, allowing the lens to become more spherical (thicker) for near focus.

questions.text: Which ocular structure has no photoreceptors ?
questions.explanation: The optic disc is where ganglion cell axons converge to exit as the optic nerve, and it contains no photoreceptors — hence the blind spot. The fovea, in contrast, has the highest photoreceptor (cone) density.

questions.text: All of the following are parts of the uvea EXCEPT:
options: None of the above — all are part of the uvea
originalOptions: None of the above — all are part of the uvea
questions.explanation: The uveal tract comprises the iris, ciliary body, and choroid — the middle vascular coat. The retina is the inner neural coat, a separate layer of the globe wall.

questions.text: Improvement of vision with a pinhole test suggests which underlying cause of reduced visual acuity?
questions.explanation: A pinhole eliminates the effect of uncorrected refractive error by narrowing the bundle of light rays reaching the retina, improving focus. Vision that does not improve with a pinhole points instead toward organic pathology like dense cataract or macular/optic nerve disease.

questions.text: Commotio retinae is seen in:
questions.explanation: According to Ophthalmology Book, commotio retinae is typically observed following a closed eye injury, or concussion injury. In such cases, areas of retinal haemorrhage may be seen alongside the characteristic patches of white, retinal oedema known as commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema). This mechanical disruption of the photoreceptor outer segments is caused by blunt contusion and is entirely unrelated to papilloedema or retinal vascular occlusions.

questions.text: A patient with an eye injury is managed with 30 minutes of irrigation, then referred to the clinic/office for further assessment. This management sequence is most appropriate for which type of ocular trauma?
questions.explanation: Chemical injury requires immediate irrigation for a minimum of 15–30 minutes before history-taking or formal examination — treatment begins before everything else.

questions.text: What is the abnormality shown in the image? [img: subconjunctivalhaemorrhage.png ]
questions.explanation: A well-demarcated, flat, bright red patch of blood tracking under the conjunctiva, usually benign and self-limiting, is a subconjunctival haemorrhage.

questions.text: A patient presents with a hazy cornea following an alkali burn. What is the diagnosis, and what is the immediate first step in management? [img: hazycornea.png ]
questions.explanation: Irrigation must begin immediately, before history or examination. Once the eye is irrigated and pH neutral, ongoing treatment includes topical antibiotics, cautious steroids, and oral/topical vitamin C plus tetracyclines to support healing and prevent corneal melting.

questions.text: A 48-year-old mechanic was using a pneumatic pump to lift a vehicle when a pipe burst, blowing air at 150 psi onto his left eye. He now has blurred vision and pain. On slit-lamp examination, the inferior half of the anterior chamber appears red, and superiorly the pupil is irregular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
originalOptions: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
questions.correctAnswer: E) Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
questions.correctAnswerText: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
questions.explanation: Blood layering inferiorly in the anterior chamber is hyphema from torn iris/ciliary vessels, and an irregular pupil after blunt trauma reflects traumatic mydriasis/iris sphincter tears — both classic findings after a high-pressure blunt blast injury to the eye.

questions.text: A 56-year-old man develops a sudden, bright red patch on the white of his left eye. He has had a chest infection recently. The eye is slightly sore but his vision is unaffected. What is shown, and what is the appropriate management? [img: subconjunctivalhaemorrhagechestinfection.png ]
questions.correctAnswer: E) Subconjunctival haemorrhage; reassurance, usually self-limiting
questions.explanation: Recent chest infection is a clue toward vigorous coughing, which raises intrathoracic and venous pressure, transmitted back to the delicate conjunctival capillaries and causing one to rupture. This produces a benign, self-limiting subconjunctival haemorrhage — alarming in appearance but not sight-threatening, resolving over 1–2 weeks without treatment.

questions.text: After an orbital floor fracture, a patient is unable to look up or down. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The inferior rectus is classically entrapped in an orbital floor fracture; a physically tethered muscle can restrict movement in both directions, confirmed with a positive forced duction test.

questions.text: A patient presents with a history of blunt ocular trauma. Which secondary condition is this patient at a lifelong, delayed risk of developing, necessitating permanent monitoring?
questions.explanation: Blunt ocular trauma can cause angle recession, which is a tear within the ciliary body face at the drainage angle. While often initially asymptomatic, this structural damage carries a lifelong risk of delayed-onset glaucoma (sometimes appearing years after the injury), which requires permanent intraocular pressure (IOP) monitoring. Although traumatic cataract is also a recognized complication of blunt trauma, the specific mention of "delayed/lifelong risk" classically identifies secondary glaucoma as the intended answer.

questions.text: Best initial treatment for traumatic hyphema:
options: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
originalOptions: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
questions.correctAnswerText: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
questions.explanation: Initial management is rest with the head elevated, a protective shield, and cycloplegics, treating any IOP rise; aspirin/NSAIDs must be avoided as they worsen bleeding. Surgical washout is reserved only for non-clearing hyphema or uncontrolled IOP.

questions.text: For a suspected penetrating (open-globe) eye injury, what is the first step in management?
options: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
originalOptions: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
questions.correctAnswer: C) Protect the eye with a rigid shield
questions.correctAnswerText: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
questions.explanation: A rigid protective shield (never a pressure pad) should be placed immediately, alongside stopping further examination, keeping the patient fasted, and urgent referral.

questions.text: After ocular trauma, a peaked or teardrop-shaped pupil suggests what diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A peaked, teardrop, or irregular pupil points toward the site of a leak/uveal prolapse and is a red-flag sign of open globe injury.

questions.text: Penetrating eye trauma most commonly causes:
questions.correctAnswer: B) Iris prolapse and pupil distortion
questions.explanation: Visible uveal tissue (iris/ciliary body) prolapsing through the wound, with resulting pupil distortion, is a hallmark open-globe red flag requiring immediate shield and urgent surgical referral.

questions.text: Hyphema is blood in the:
questions.explanation: Hyphema refers to blood accumulation in the anterior chamber of the eye, usually resulting from severe trauma that tears iris or ciliary body vessels.

questions.text: Most important complication of traumatic hyphema is:
questions.explanation: If intraocular pressure rises while blood remains in the anterior chamber for a prolonged period, hemoglobin deposits within the corneal tissue (blood staining), causing permanent opacification that may later require corneal transplantation.

questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in blunt trauma to the eye?
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma causes closed injuries (contusions, internal tears), not double perforation, which is characteristic of penetrating injuries.

questions.text: Blow-out fracture of orbit commonly produces:
questions.correctAnswer: D) Fracture of floor of orbit
questions.explanation: An orbital blow-out fracture occurs when blunt force increases intraorbital pressure, causing the thinnest walls of the orbit to break while the rim remains intact. The orbital floor is the most common site for this fracture, often leading to the herniation or entrapment of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus.

questions.text: The sure sign of scleral rupture is:
questions.explanation: Visible prolapse of intraocular contents (such as uveal tissue or vitreous) through the site of rupture is the definitive, conclusive sign of scleral rupture, while the other signs are supportive but not conclusive on their own.

questions.text: A patient received a tennis ball hit to his eye which used to have 6/6 vision. External eye examination showed no abnormalities, vision is HM, and red reflex is normal. Possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Severe blunt trauma from a large spherical object (a tennis ball) causes retinal concussion (Berlin's edema) despite an externally normal anterior segment and a normal red reflex (since the vitreous and lens are intact), explaining the acute drop in vision.

questions.text: Vossius ring, seen after blunt ocular trauma, refers to a ring of iris pigment deposited on which structure?
questions.explanation: A Vossius ring is a circular imprint of iris pigment on the anterior lens capsule, caused by the pupil margin striking the lens during acute blunt trauma. It is a useful sign confirming previous significant blunt ocular injury.

questions.text: Adhesion of iris margin anteriorly is known as:
questions.explanation: Adhesion of the iris margin to the cornea (or the anterior chamber angle) is called anterior synechia, and often occurs after trauma, chronic inflammation, or surgery.

questions.text: Dense scar of cornea with incarceration of iris is known as:
questions.explanation: When iris tissue becomes incorporated into a dense corneal scar (usually after corneal perforation), the condition is called "adherent leucoma (Leucoma adherent)" to distinguish it from simple dense leucoma not attached to the iris.

questions.text: The first line of treatment in acid burns of the eye is:
options: Instilling a drop of oil in the eye
Instilling a drop of surface anesthetic into the eye
originalOptions: Instilling a drop of oil in the eye
Instilling a drop of surface anesthetic into the eye
questions.correctAnswer: C) Immediate wash with plain water
questions.explanation: In any chemical burn (acid or alkali), the absolute top priority is immediate, copious irrigation with water or saline to dilute and remove the caustic substance before any other procedure, because every minute of delay increases the depth of injury.

questions.text: An 8-year-old girl received a tennis ball trauma to her right eye. On examination on the same day you would find:
questions.explanation: Bleeding into the anterior chamber (hyphema) is the direct, early sign expected on the same day as an acute blunt trauma, while corneal blood staining is a delayed complication that only occurs if elevated pressure with blood persists for a prolonged period.

questions.text: A patient with a history of sarcoidosis presents with redness and photophobia in his right eye for the past 3 weeks. He was initially treated with topical Gentamicin, but his symptoms did not improve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous uveitis, which does not respond to an antibiotic like gentamicin since it is not a bacterial infection. Persistent redness/photophobia despite antibiotic treatment in a sarcoidosis patient points strongly to uveitis.

questions.text: In a cataract post-operative clinic, a 62-year-old gentleman complains that since the operation he sees floaters and flashing lights, and yesterday a "curtain descended over part of his vision." He worries the cataract operation failed. What should he be told?
options: Reassure him that this is normal following cataract surgery, and vision can take weeks to improve
Reassure him that he does not require surgery; he will require a course of steroids
Reassure him that a short course of topical antibiotics should be sufficient
It is likely he will require further surgery, needing a new intraocular lens as the previous implant failed
It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
originalOptions: Reassure him that this is normal following cataract surgery, and vision can take weeks to improve
Reassure him that he does not require surgery; he will require a course of steroids
Reassure him that a short course of topical antibiotics should be sufficient
It is likely he will require further surgery, needing a new intraocular lens as the previous implant failed
It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
questions.correctAnswer: E) It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
questions.correctAnswerText: It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
questions.explanation: Floaters, flashes, and a curtain/shadow are the classic triad of retinal detachment (a known complication after cataract surgery, related to PVD), not a normal post-operative finding. This requires urgent retinal detachment surgery — a different operation from the original phacoemulsification.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with uveitis?
options: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
originalOptions: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
questions.correctAnswer: B) Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
questions.correctAnswerText: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
questions.explanation: Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) is an HLA-B27-associated cause of acute anterior uveitis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis classically causes chronic, silent anterior uveitis in children. Pancoast tumour is associated with Horner syndrome, not uveitis.

questions.text: Regarding the ciliary body, which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: It is continuous with the iris anteriorly and the choroid posteriorly
The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
The ciliary epithelium produces aqueous humour
originalOptions: It is continuous with the iris anteriorly and the choroid posteriorly
The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
The ciliary epithelium produces aqueous humour
questions.correctAnswer: B) The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
questions.correctAnswerText: The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
questions.explanation: The ciliary body consists of both the pars plicata (aqueous-producing processes) and the pars plana, not the pars plana alone — describing it as composed entirely of the pars plana is false. A, C, and D are accurate descriptions of ciliary body anatomy and function.

questions.text: Which of the following medications is NOT indicated in the treatment of anterior uveitis?
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, which promotes posterior synechiae formation in an already inflamed eye — cycloplegics (cyclopentolate, atropine) are used instead to keep the pupil moving and prevent synechiae.

questions.text: All of the following are recognised complications of anterior uveitis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cataract, secondary glaucoma (from synechiae/trabecular blockage), and iris atrophy (as in Fuchs' heterochromic uveitis) are recognised complications of anterior uveitis. Retinal detachment is not a typical direct complication of anterior chamber inflammation.

questions.text: Which of the following organisms/causes is classically associated with both keratitis and uveitis in the same patient?
questions.explanation: HSV can cause both dendritic keratitis and an associated anterior uveitis/iridocyclitis as part of the same recurrent infection, reflecting shared viral involvement of the anterior segment.

questions.text: Which of the following is one of the earliest features of anterior uveitis on slit-lamp examination?
questions.explanation: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber are the direct, earliest sign of active inflammation, appearing before keratic precipitates, synechiae, or hypopyon develop with more established or severe disease.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT occur in uveitis?
options: Posterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the lens and bind down the pupil
Anterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the trabecular meshwork or cornea, occluding the drainage angle
originalOptions: Posterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the lens and bind down the pupil
Anterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the trabecular meshwork or cornea, occluding the drainage angle
questions.explanation: Hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber, classically from trauma, not a feature of uveitis. Hypopyon (white cells), synechiae, and raised IOP (from synechiae/inflammatory debris blocking outflow) are all recognised uveitis findings.

questions.text: A 23-year-old Caucasian man with acutely painful red eye, photophobia, and morning-stiffness lower back pain. Which of the following statements is FALSE? [img: caucasianmananterioruveitis.png ]
options: The diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
Keratic precipitates and hypopyon are expected findings
The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
Treatment includes topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics
originalOptions: The diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
Keratic precipitates and hypopyon are expected findings
The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
Treatment includes topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics
questions.correctAnswer: C) The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
questions.correctAnswerText: The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
questions.explanation: This presentation — acute pain, photophobia, and a red eye — is classic for anterior uveitis, not intermediate uveitis, which typically presents with painless floaters and vitritis rather than an acutely painful red eye.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with a yellowish retinal lesion and necrosis. The likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: CMV retinitis presents as a necrotising retinitis with haemorrhage (classically described as a "pizza-pie" fundus), typically in significantly immunosuppressed patients, and needs systemic antiviral treatment.

questions.text: A 56-year-old lady with known sarcoidosis on systemic prednisolone presents with photophobia, redness, and blurred vision, with no previous eye history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a classic cause of granulomatous uveitis, and the triad of photophobia, redness, and blurred vision fits anterior uveitis rather than the milder discomfort of episcleritis, the external picture of bacterial conjunctivitis, or a traumatic corneal abrasion.

questions.text: In anterior uveitis, the pupil is generally:
questions.explanation: Inflammation causes miosis, and posterior synechiae (iris adhering to the anterior lens capsule) produce an irregular, poorly dilating pupil — a hallmark finding in anterior uveitis, distinct from the fixed, mid-dilated pupil of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.text: A case of anterior uveitis is shown, with ciliary (limbal) injection and keratic precipitates visible on the corneal endothelium. This presentation is most consistent with an underlying joint disease. The full findings, differential diagnoses, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: anterioruveitis3images.png ]
questions.explanation: Findings — ciliary (limbal) injection and keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium. Differential diagnoses — ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile chronic arthritis, reactive arthritis (Reiter's disease). Treatment — topical corticosteroids plus mydriatics/cycloplegics (e.g., cyclopentolate or atropine drops).

questions.text: A 23-year-old Caucasian man presents with an acutely painful, red right eye and marked photophobia. History reveals lower back pain for several months, with morning stiffness. The diagnosis, key findings, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: caucasianmananterioruveitis.png ]
questions.explanation: Diagnosis — acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27-related). Key findings — keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and hypopyon (a pus layer in the anterior chamber). Treatment — topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics/mydriatics.

questions.text: A 23-year-old man with backache and oral ulcers is referred with right eye pain and photophobia, and a history of previous mild blurred vision episodes. The pathological findings, differential diagnoses, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: hypopyon23keraticprecipitates.png ]
questions.explanation: Findings — hypopyon (accumulation of white cells in the anterior chamber inferiorly) and keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium, indicating acute anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis). Differential diagnoses — Behçet's disease (most likely, given oral ulcers and young age), ankylosing spondylitis (associated with backache and HLA-B27), inflammatory bowel disease-associated uveitis / reactive arthritis / sarcoidosis. Treatments — topical or systemic corticosteroids, and topical cycloplegics/mydriatics (e.g., atropine).

questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with a painful red eye and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination shows keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and posterior synechiae, with the iris adherent to the anterior lens capsule producing an irregular pupil. Which of the following statements about this presentation is FALSE?
options: Keratic precipitates are deposits of inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium
Posterior synechiae is adhesion of the iris to the anterior lens capsule
This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
Cycloplegics help prevent further synechiae formation
originalOptions: Keratic precipitates are deposits of inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium
Posterior synechiae is adhesion of the iris to the anterior lens capsule
This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
Cycloplegics help prevent further synechiae formation
questions.correctAnswer: C) This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
questions.correctAnswerText: This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
questions.explanation: Keratic precipitates and posterior synechiae are findings of anterior uveitis, not intermediate uveitis, which instead presents with vitritis and floaters without these anterior segment signs.

questions.text: Arrange the five histological layers of the cornea in correct anterior-to-posterior order:
options: Epithelium → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Endothelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Epithelium
Epithelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Endothelium
Bowman's layer → Epithelium → Stroma → Endothelium → Descemet's membrane
originalOptions: Epithelium → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Endothelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Epithelium
Epithelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Endothelium
Bowman's layer → Epithelium → Stroma → Endothelium → Descemet's membrane
questions.correctAnswer: B) Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
questions.correctAnswerText: Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
questions.explanation: The correct anterior-to-posterior sequence is epithelium (regenerates fast) → Bowman's layer (does not regenerate) → stroma (~90% of thickness) → Descemet's membrane (basement membrane) → endothelium (pump layer, does not regenerate).

questions.text: The main route of aqueous humour outflow, accounting for approximately 90–96% of drainage, is:
options: The uveoscleral pathway through the ciliary body face
The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
originalOptions: The uveoscleral pathway through the ciliary body face
The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
questions.correctAnswer: C) The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
questions.correctAnswerText: The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
questions.explanation: Aqueous drains conventionally through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal and then into episcleral veins, accounting for the large majority of outflow; the uveoscleral route handles only about 4–10%. This conventional pathway is the main pharmacological target in glaucoma treatment.

questions.text: Which structure is responsible for producing the outer lipid layer of the tear film, and what is its main function?
options: Lacrimal gland; provides 90% of tear thickness
Goblet cells; wets the hydrophobic corneal epithelium
Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
Accessory lacrimal glands; delivers antibacterial proteins
originalOptions: Lacrimal gland; provides 90% of tear thickness
Goblet cells; wets the hydrophobic corneal epithelium
Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
Accessory lacrimal glands; delivers antibacterial proteins
questions.correctAnswer: C) Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
questions.correctAnswerText: Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
questions.explanation: The meibomian glands, located within the tarsal plates, secrete the outer lipid layer whose main job is to slow evaporation of the underlying aqueous layer. Dysfunction of these glands is a major cause of evaporative dry eye.

questions.text: Contraction of which iris muscle produces mydriasis, and via which autonomic pathway?
questions.explanation: The dilator pupillae consists of radial fibres under sympathetic control, producing mydriasis, whereas the sphincter pupillae is circular and parasympathetically innervated (CN III), producing miosis.

questions.text: Cones, responsible for colour vision and fine visual acuity, are exclusively found at which retinal location?
questions.explanation: Cones are concentrated at the macula and are exclusively present at its centre, the fovea centralis, which is the point of sharpest vision. Rods, by contrast, are far more numerous but absent from the very centre of the fovea, mediating dim-light and peripheral vision instead.

questions.text: The optic disc corresponds to the physiological blind spot because:
options: It is the thinnest part of the retina
It is where the vitreous attaches most firmly
originalOptions: It is the thinnest part of the retina
It is where the vitreous attaches most firmly
questions.explanation: The optic disc is where retinal ganglion cell axons converge and exit the eye as the optic nerve; since it contains no photoreceptors, it corresponds to the physiological blind spot. This is distinct from the fovea, which has the highest photoreceptor density.

questions.text: The vitreous body is firmly attached at all of the following sites EXCEPT:
options: The vitreous base, just behind the ora serrata
None of the above — all are correct attachment sites
originalOptions: The vitreous base, just behind the ora serrata
None of the above — all are correct attachment sites
questions.explanation: The vitreous body is attached to the vitreous base (peripheral retina/pars plana), the optic disc margin, and the macula. While its attachment to the macula and retinal vessels is relatively less firm than at the base or disc, it remains a critical attachment site. These locations are clinically significant because they experience traction and pulling when the vitreous shrinks with age. The lens equator is not a vitreous attachment site.

questions.text: The conjunctiva contains goblet cells whose function is to:
options: Produce the outer lipid layer of the tear film
Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
Provide sensory innervation to the ocular surface
originalOptions: Produce the outer lipid layer of the tear film
Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
Provide sensory innervation to the ocular surface
questions.correctAnswer: B) Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
questions.correctAnswerText: Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
questions.explanation: Goblet cells within the conjunctiva secrete mucin, which allows the aqueous tear layer to wet the otherwise hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly. The conjunctiva itself has bulbar and palpebral parts meeting at the fornices.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct pairing of a uveal tract structure with its principal role?
options: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
originalOptions: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
questions.correctAnswer: B) Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
questions.correctAnswerText: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
questions.explanation: The choroid is the posterior, vascular part of the uveal tract, and its capillary layer (the choriocapillaris) supplies the outer retina, including the photoreceptors. New vessel growth from the choroid through Bruch's membrane is also the underlying mechanism of wet age-related macular degeneration.

questions.text: Select all correct statements regarding the three concentric layers of the globe:
options: The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera
The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid
The inner neural coat is the retina
The lens forms part of the outer fibrous coat
The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
originalOptions: The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera
The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid
The inner neural coat is the retina
The lens forms part of the outer fibrous coat
The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
questions.correctAnswer: A) The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera / B) The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid / C) The inner neural coat is the retina / E) The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
questions.correctAnswerText: A) The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera / B) The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid / C) The inner neural coat is the retina / E) The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
questions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are all true — the globe wall consists of an outer fibrous coat (cornea + sclera), a middle vascular coat (uveal tract: iris + ciliary body + choroid), and an inner neural coat (retina). D is false because the lens is one of the three transparent refracting media inside the globe (with aqueous humour and vitreous), not part of the wall itself.

allQuestions.text: Select all the correct statements regarding the Cornea:
options: Has an endothelial layer that regenerates readily.
Has an epithelial layer that fails to regenerate.
The endothelium actively pumps water from the stroma.
Is an important refractive component of the eye.
Has a stroma composed of randomly arranged collagen fibrils.
originalOptions: Has an endothelial layer that regenerates readily.
Has an epithelial layer that fails to regenerate.
The endothelium actively pumps water from the stroma.
Is an important refractive component of the eye.
Has a stroma composed of randomly arranged collagen fibrils.
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The endothelium actively pumps water from the stroma. / D) Is an important refractive component of the eye.
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: C) The endothelium actively pumps water from the stroma. / D) Is an important refractive component of the eye.
allQuestions.explanation: A) False. The human endothelium does not regenerate; dead cells are replaced by the spreading of surviving cells. B) False. The epithelial layer readily regenerates. C) True. The endothelial cells pump out ions and the water follows osmotically. Removal of water maintains corneal transparency. D) True. The cornea is a more powerful refractive element than the natural lens of the eye. E) False. The fine, equally spaced, stromal collagen fibrils are arranged in parallel and packed in an orderly manner. This is a requirement for transparency.

allQuestions.groupName: Anatomy of the Eye - Book questions

allQuestions.text: Select all the correct statements regarding the Retina:
options: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve.
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision.
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the retinal pigment epithelium.
The RPE delivers vitamin A for rhodopsin production.
originalOptions: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve.
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision.
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the retinal pigment epithelium.
The RPE delivers vitamin A for rhodopsin production.
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Is ten layers thick. / B) Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve. / E) The RPE delivers vitamin A for rhodopsin production.
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A) Is ten layers thick. / B) Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve. / E) The RPE delivers vitamin A for rhodopsin production.
allQuestions.explanation: A) True. B) True. The retinal ganglion cell axons form the retinal nerve fibre layer and exit the eye at the optic nerve head. C) False. The rods are responsible for night vision and three cone types are responsible for daylight and colour vision. D) False. The attachment is loose; the neuroretina separates from the RPE in retinal detachment. E) True. Vitamin A is delivered by the RPE to the photoreceptors and combined with opsin.

allQuestions.groupName: Anatomy of the Eye - Book questions

allQuestions.text: Select all the correct statements regarding the Lens:
options: Is surrounded by a collagenous capsule.
Cortex and nucleus are rich in organelles.
Has a high refractive index owing to its protein content.
Shape becomes more curved during accommodation for near.
originalOptions: Is surrounded by a collagenous capsule.
Cortex and nucleus are rich in organelles.
Has a high refractive index owing to its protein content.
Shape becomes more curved during accommodation for near.
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Grows throughout life. / B) Is surrounded by a collagenous capsule. / D) Has a high refractive index owing to its protein content. / E) Shape becomes more curved during accommodation for near.
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A) Grows throughout life. / B) Is surrounded by a collagenous capsule. / D) Has a high refractive index owing to its protein content. / E) Shape becomes more curved during accommodation for near.
allQuestions.explanation: A) True. It does grow throughout life. B) True. This is of great importance in cataract surgery. C) False. The older, deep cortical and nuclear fibres lose their nuclei and other organelles. D) True. The high protein content accounts for its high refractive index. E) True.

options: Attaches the lens to the ciliary body.
Is part of the iridocorneal angle.
Transmits changes in tension to the lens capsule.
originalOptions: Attaches the lens to the ciliary body.
Is part of the iridocorneal angle.
Transmits changes in tension to the lens capsule.

allQuestions.explanation: The tear film is trilaminar (lipid, aqueous, mucin), with the inner mucin layer directly wetting the hydrophobic corneal epithelium — making C correct and B wrong (three layers, not four). A is wrong because the tear film average thickness is only 3 µm (ranging from 2 to 5.5 µm), not 100 µm. D is wrong because the tear-air interface is actually a major refractive surface of the eye, so the tear film is optically important, not irrelevant.

allQuestions.text: Aqueous humour is formed by:
allQuestions.explanation: B and C are wrong because the iris and lens play no role in aqueous production — the iris only regulates pupil size, and the lens is purely refractive. D is a plausible-sounding distractor since the pars plana is part of the ciliary body region, but production occurs at the ciliary processes (pars plicata), not the pars plana. E is wrong because the trabecular meshwork is a drainage structure, not a secretory one.

allQuestions.text: All of the following statements about the tear film are true EXCEPT:
options: Lysozyme and lactoferrin in the aqueous layer provide antibacterial protection
The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
The tear film keeps the corneal surface smooth, clear, and lubricated
Conjunctival goblet cells produce the inner mucin layer
The mucin layer allows the aqueous layer to wet the hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly

The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
The tear film keeps the corneal surface smooth, clear, and lubricated
Conjunctival goblet cells produce the inner mucin layer
The mucin layer allows the aqueous layer to wet the hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The meibomian glands produce the aqueous layer of the tear film
allQuestions.explanation: The meibomian glands, located in the tarsal plates, secrete the outer lipid layer of the tear film, not the aqueous layer — the aqueous layer (about 90% of tear thickness) comes from the main and accessory lacrimal glands, and also carries antibacterial proteins like lysozyme and lactoferrin. A, C, D, and E are all correct descriptions of tear film anatomy.

allQuestions.text: Choose the correct answer about the retina:
options: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the RPE
The RPE delivers vitamin K for rhodopsin production
originalOptions: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
Has three types of rods responsible for colour vision
The neuroretina is firmly attached to the RPE
The RPE delivers vitamin K for rhodopsin production
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Has ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve
allQuestions.explanation: The retinal ganglion cell axons converge at the optic disc and exit the eye as the optic nerve — this is why the optic disc, lacking photoreceptors, corresponds to the physiological blind spot. A is wrong because the retina has 10 histological layers, not 7. C is wrong on two counts: colour vision is mediated by cones (not rods), and there are three types of cones (not rods). D is wrong because the neurosensory retina is only loosely apposed to the RPE (not firmly attached) — this is exactly why retinal detachment can occur. E is wrong because the RPE recycles vitamin A (not vitamin K) for the visual cycle and rhodopsin regeneration.

allQuestions.text: Most of the thickness of the cornea is formed by:
allQuestions.explanation: The stroma (substantia propria) makes up about 90% of corneal thickness. It consists of organized collagen fibers that give the cornea its transparency and structural strength.

allQuestions.text: Cornea is supplied by nerve fibers derived from:
allQuestions.explanation: The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues in the body, supplied sensorially by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve — which is why corneal inflammation or ulceration is extremely painful.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is not a source of nutrients to the cornea?
allQuestions.explanation: The cornea is avascular and is nourished by atmospheric oxygen, the aqueous humour, and the perilimbal capillary network. The vitreous humour is not a source of corneal nutrition.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are avascular EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are vascular
originalOptions: All of the above are vascular
allQuestions.explanation: The cornea and lens are explicitly avascular, nourished only by diffusion, and the vitreous is a clear gel with no vessels of its own. The sclera is a hypovascular collagenous coat. While it has a very limited internal blood supply, it is pierced by blood vessels and intimately connected to the overlying vascularised episclera, making it the only structure listed that is not completely avascular. Note: if option E had instead read "All of the above are avascular," E would be the more correct choice, since the sclera is technically hypovascular rather than completely avascular.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are part of the uvea except:
allQuestions.explanation: The uvea consists of the iris, ciliary body (which has two parts: pars plicata and pars plana), and the choroid. Schwalbe's line is an anatomical landmark at the anterior chamber angle (the termination of Descemet's membrane) and is not part of the uveal tract.

allQuestions.text: The following is a part of uvea except:
allQuestions.explanation: Bowman's membrane is a layer of the cornea and has no relation to the uveal tract.

allQuestions.text: Optic disc diameter is:
allQuestions.explanation: The optic disc diameter is used as a standard unit of measurement (Disc Diameter, DD) to describe the size and location of fundus lesions.

allQuestions.text: Aqueous humor is secreted by:
allQuestions.explanation: The ciliary processes are the precise anatomical site of aqueous humour secretion within the ciliary body.

allQuestions.text: Corneal ulceration/anaesthesia is caused by injury to the ___ cranial nerve:
allQuestions.explanation: Loss of corneal sensation (from trigeminal nerve injury) abolishes the protective blink reflex, leaving the cornea vulnerable to neurotrophic keratitis.

allQuestions.text: Number of layers in the neurosensory retina is:
allQuestions.explanation: The neurosensory retina classically consists of 9 layers, from the photoreceptors to the nerve fiber layer. The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is anatomically and functionally a separate, tenth layer.

allQuestions.text: During accommodation for near vision, which of the following changes occurs?
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens

The pupil dilates and the lens flattens
The cornea steepens while the lens remains unchanged

allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker
allQuestions.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonular fibres, allowing the lens to become more spherical (thicker) for near focus.

allQuestions.text: Which ocular structure has no photoreceptors ?
allQuestions.explanation: The optic disc is where ganglion cell axons converge to exit as the optic nerve, and it contains no photoreceptors — hence the blind spot. The fovea, in contrast, has the highest photoreceptor (cone) density.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are parts of the uvea EXCEPT:
options: None of the above — all are part of the uvea
originalOptions: None of the above — all are part of the uvea
allQuestions.explanation: The uveal tract comprises the iris, ciliary body, and choroid — the middle vascular coat. The retina is the inner neural coat, a separate layer of the globe wall.

allQuestions.text: Improvement of vision with a pinhole test suggests which underlying cause of reduced visual acuity?
allQuestions.explanation: A pinhole eliminates the effect of uncorrected refractive error by narrowing the bundle of light rays reaching the retina, improving focus. Vision that does not improve with a pinhole points instead toward organic pathology like dense cataract or macular/optic nerve disease.

allQuestions.text: A 24-year-old man presents after blunt trauma to his right eye. He complains of vertical diplopia, especially on looking up. CT scan shows a right orbital floor fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: Entrapment of the inferior rectus limits elevation of the affected eye
Hypoaesthesia over the cheek may occur due to infraorbital nerve injury
The squint decreases when the patient looks upward
CT scan is the investigation of choice

Hypoaesthesia over the cheek may occur due to infraorbital nerve injury

allQuestions.explanation: Entrapment classically limits elevation, so the diplopia/squint worsens (not decreases) on upgaze. A, B, C, and E are all accurate — infraorbital nerve runs through the floor, and CT with coronal cuts is the imaging of choice.

allQuestions.text: What is the diagnosis shown in the image? [img: hyphema.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Hyphema is blood layering in the anterior chamber from blunt trauma tearing iris/ciliary body vessels, graded from a thin layer to a total "eight-ball" hyphema. Hypopyon, by contrast, is a layer of white cells, not blood.

allQuestions.text: A patient was hit with a tennis ball. Which of the following is NOT true? [img: orbitalfloorfracture.png ]
options: Diplopia is relieved when the patient looks upward
Restricted eye movement, classically limited upgaze, may occur
CT with coronal cuts is the investigation of choice

originalOptions: Diplopia is relieved when the patient looks upward

CT with coronal cuts is the investigation of choice
