allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Diplopia is relieved when the patient looks upward
allQuestions.explanation: Diplopia worsens, not relieves, on upgaze due to inferior rectus/fat entrapment limiting elevation. B, C, D, and E are all accurate features of orbital floor fracture.

allQuestions.text: Commotio retinae is seen in:
allQuestions.explanation: According to Ophthalmology Book, commotio retinae is typically observed following a closed eye injury, or concussion injury. In such cases, areas of retinal haemorrhage may be seen alongside the characteristic patches of white, retinal oedema known as commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema). This mechanical disruption of the photoreceptor outer segments is caused by blunt contusion and is entirely unrelated to papilloedema or retinal vascular occlusions.

allQuestions.text: Select all correct statements regarding hyphaema:
options: Is a fluid collection of white cells in the anterior chamber
May be associated with a low intraocular pressure
Is treated with restriction of activity
If it recurs within a short time, may result in more severe problems
originalOptions: Is a fluid collection of white cells in the anterior chamber
May be associated with a low intraocular pressure
Is treated with restriction of activity
If it recurs within a short time, may result in more severe problems
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Is treated with restriction of activity / D) If it recurs within a short time, may result in more severe problems / E) Is treated with steroid drops
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: C) Is treated with restriction of activity / D) If it recurs within a short time, may result in more severe problems / E) Is treated with steroid drops
allQuestions.explanation: A is false — hyphema is blood, not white cells (white cells = hypopyon). B is false — hyphema is associated with raised IOP (blood blocks the trabecular meshwork), not low IOP. C is true — rest/activity restriction is standard management. D is true — re-bleeding (typically day 2–5) is often worse than the original bleed with higher complication risk. E is true — These will help to reduce any associated inflammation and reduce the incidence of rebleeds.

allQuestions.text: A patient with an eye injury is managed with 30 minutes of irrigation, then referred to the clinic/office for further assessment. This management sequence is most appropriate for which type of ocular trauma?
allQuestions.explanation: Chemical injury requires immediate irrigation for a minimum of 15–30 minutes before history-taking or formal examination — treatment begins before everything else.

allQuestions.text: What is the abnormality shown in the image? [img: subconjunctivalhaemorrhage.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: A well-demarcated, flat, bright red patch of blood tracking under the conjunctiva, usually benign and self-limiting, is a subconjunctival haemorrhage.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with a hazy cornea following an alkali burn. What is the diagnosis, and what is the immediate first step in management? [img: hazycornea.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Irrigation must begin immediately, before history or examination. Once the eye is irrigated and pH neutral, ongoing treatment includes topical antibiotics, cautious steroids, and oral/topical vitamin C plus tetracyclines to support healing and prevent corneal melting.

allQuestions.text: A 48-year-old mechanic was using a pneumatic pump to lift a vehicle when a pipe burst, blowing air at 150 psi onto his left eye. He now has blurred vision and pain. On slit-lamp examination, the inferior half of the anterior chamber appears red, and superiorly the pupil is irregular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
originalOptions: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hyphema with traumatic iris sphincter tear
allQuestions.explanation: Blood layering inferiorly in the anterior chamber is hyphema from torn iris/ciliary vessels, and an irregular pupil after blunt trauma reflects traumatic mydriasis/iris sphincter tears — both classic findings after a high-pressure blunt blast injury to the eye.

allQuestions.text: A 56-year-old man develops a sudden, bright red patch on the white of his left eye. He has had a chest infection recently. The eye is slightly sore but his vision is unaffected. What is shown, and what is the appropriate management? [img: subconjunctivalhaemorrhagechestinfection.png ]
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Subconjunctival haemorrhage; reassurance, usually self-limiting
allQuestions.explanation: Recent chest infection is a clue toward vigorous coughing, which raises intrathoracic and venous pressure, transmitted back to the delicate conjunctival capillaries and causing one to rupture. This produces a benign, self-limiting subconjunctival haemorrhage — alarming in appearance but not sight-threatening, resolving over 1–2 weeks without treatment.

allQuestions.text: After an orbital floor fracture, a patient is unable to look up or down. What is the most likely cause?
allQuestions.explanation: The inferior rectus is classically entrapped in an orbital floor fracture; a physically tethered muscle can restrict movement in both directions, confirmed with a positive forced duction test.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with a history of blunt ocular trauma. Which secondary condition is this patient at a lifelong, delayed risk of developing, necessitating permanent monitoring?
allQuestions.explanation: Blunt ocular trauma can cause angle recession, which is a tear within the ciliary body face at the drainage angle. While often initially asymptomatic, this structural damage carries a lifelong risk of delayed-onset glaucoma (sometimes appearing years after the injury), which requires permanent intraocular pressure (IOP) monitoring. Although traumatic cataract is also a recognized complication of blunt trauma, the specific mention of "delayed/lifelong risk" classically identifies secondary glaucoma as the intended answer.

allQuestions.text: Best initial treatment for traumatic hyphema:
options: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
originalOptions: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bed rest and cycloplegics with head elevation
allQuestions.explanation: Initial management is rest with the head elevated, a protective shield, and cycloplegics, treating any IOP rise; aspirin/NSAIDs must be avoided as they worsen bleeding. Surgical washout is reserved only for non-clearing hyphema or uncontrolled IOP.

allQuestions.text: For a suspected penetrating (open-globe) eye injury, what is the first step in management?
options: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
originalOptions: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Protect the eye with a rigid shield
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Protect the eye with a rigid shield
allQuestions.explanation: A rigid protective shield (never a pressure pad) should be placed immediately, alongside stopping further examination, keeping the patient fasted, and urgent referral.

allQuestions.text: After ocular trauma, a peaked or teardrop-shaped pupil suggests what diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A peaked, teardrop, or irregular pupil points toward the site of a leak/uveal prolapse and is a red-flag sign of open globe injury.

allQuestions.text: Penetrating eye trauma most commonly causes:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Iris prolapse and pupil distortion
allQuestions.explanation: Visible uveal tissue (iris/ciliary body) prolapsing through the wound, with resulting pupil distortion, is a hallmark open-globe red flag requiring immediate shield and urgent surgical referral.

allQuestions.text: Hyphema is blood in the:
allQuestions.explanation: Hyphema refers to blood accumulation in the anterior chamber of the eye, usually resulting from severe trauma that tears iris or ciliary body vessels.

allQuestions.text: Most important complication of traumatic hyphema is:
allQuestions.explanation: If intraocular pressure rises while blood remains in the anterior chamber for a prolonged period, hemoglobin deposits within the corneal tissue (blood staining), causing permanent opacification that may later require corneal transplantation.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is not seen in blunt trauma to the eye?
allQuestions.explanation: Blunt trauma causes closed injuries (contusions, internal tears), not double perforation, which is characteristic of penetrating injuries.

allQuestions.text: Blow-out fracture of orbit commonly produces:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Fracture of floor of orbit
allQuestions.explanation: An orbital blow-out fracture occurs when blunt force increases intraorbital pressure, causing the thinnest walls of the orbit to break while the rim remains intact. The orbital floor is the most common site for this fracture, often leading to the herniation or entrapment of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus.

allQuestions.text: The sure sign of scleral rupture is:
allQuestions.explanation: Visible prolapse of intraocular contents (such as uveal tissue or vitreous) through the site of rupture is the definitive, conclusive sign of scleral rupture, while the other signs are supportive but not conclusive on their own.

allQuestions.text: A patient received a tennis ball hit to his eye which used to have 6/6 vision. External eye examination showed no abnormalities, vision is HM, and red reflex is normal. Possible diagnosis is:
allQuestions.explanation: Severe blunt trauma from a large spherical object (a tennis ball) causes retinal concussion (Berlin's edema) despite an externally normal anterior segment and a normal red reflex (since the vitreous and lens are intact), explaining the acute drop in vision.

allQuestions.text: Vossius ring, seen after blunt ocular trauma, refers to a ring of iris pigment deposited on which structure?
allQuestions.explanation: A Vossius ring is a circular imprint of iris pigment on the anterior lens capsule, caused by the pupil margin striking the lens during acute blunt trauma. It is a useful sign confirming previous significant blunt ocular injury.

allQuestions.text: Adhesion of iris margin anteriorly is known as:
allQuestions.explanation: Adhesion of the iris margin to the cornea (or the anterior chamber angle) is called anterior synechia, and often occurs after trauma, chronic inflammation, or surgery.

allQuestions.text: Dense scar of cornea with incarceration of iris is known as:
allQuestions.explanation: When iris tissue becomes incorporated into a dense corneal scar (usually after corneal perforation), the condition is called "adherent leucoma (Leucoma adherent)" to distinguish it from simple dense leucoma not attached to the iris.

allQuestions.text: The first line of treatment in acid burns of the eye is:
options: Instilling a drop of oil in the eye
Instilling a drop of surface anesthetic into the eye
originalOptions: Instilling a drop of oil in the eye
Instilling a drop of surface anesthetic into the eye
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Immediate wash with plain water
allQuestions.explanation: In any chemical burn (acid or alkali), the absolute top priority is immediate, copious irrigation with water or saline to dilute and remove the caustic substance before any other procedure, because every minute of delay increases the depth of injury.

allQuestions.text: An 8-year-old girl received a tennis ball trauma to her right eye. On examination on the same day you would find:
allQuestions.explanation: Bleeding into the anterior chamber (hyphema) is the direct, early sign expected on the same day as an acute blunt trauma, while corneal blood staining is a delayed complication that only occurs if elevated pressure with blood persists for a prolonged period.

allQuestions.text: A patient with a history of sarcoidosis presents with redness and photophobia in his right eye for the past 3 weeks. He was initially treated with topical Gentamicin, but his symptoms did not improve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous uveitis, which does not respond to an antibiotic like gentamicin since it is not a bacterial infection. Persistent redness/photophobia despite antibiotic treatment in a sarcoidosis patient points strongly to uveitis.

allQuestions.text: In a cataract post-operative clinic, a 62-year-old gentleman complains that since the operation he sees floaters and flashing lights, and yesterday a "curtain descended over part of his vision." He worries the cataract operation failed. What should he be told?
options: Reassure him that this is normal following cataract surgery, and vision can take weeks to improve
Reassure him that he does not require surgery; he will require a course of steroids
Reassure him that a short course of topical antibiotics should be sufficient
It is likely he will require further surgery, needing a new intraocular lens as the previous implant failed
It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
originalOptions: Reassure him that this is normal following cataract surgery, and vision can take weeks to improve
Reassure him that he does not require surgery; he will require a course of steroids
Reassure him that a short course of topical antibiotics should be sufficient
It is likely he will require further surgery, needing a new intraocular lens as the previous implant failed
It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is likely he will require further surgery; however, it will not be the same operation he has had before
allQuestions.explanation: Floaters, flashes, and a curtain/shadow are the classic triad of retinal detachment (a known complication after cataract surgery, related to PVD), not a normal post-operative finding. This requires urgent retinal detachment surgery — a different operation from the original phacoemulsification.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with uveitis?
options: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
originalOptions: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Reiter's syndrome and juvenile chronic arthritis
allQuestions.explanation: Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) is an HLA-B27-associated cause of acute anterior uveitis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis classically causes chronic, silent anterior uveitis in children. Pancoast tumour is associated with Horner syndrome, not uveitis.

allQuestions.text: Regarding the ciliary body, which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: It is continuous with the iris anteriorly and the choroid posteriorly
The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
The ciliary epithelium produces aqueous humour
originalOptions: It is continuous with the iris anteriorly and the choroid posteriorly
The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
The ciliary epithelium produces aqueous humour
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The ciliary body is composed entirely of the pars plana
allQuestions.explanation: The ciliary body consists of both the pars plicata (aqueous-producing processes) and the pars plana, not the pars plana alone — describing it as composed entirely of the pars plana is false. A, C, and D are accurate descriptions of ciliary body anatomy and function.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following medications is NOT indicated in the treatment of anterior uveitis?
allQuestions.explanation: Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, which promotes posterior synechiae formation in an already inflamed eye — cycloplegics (cyclopentolate, atropine) are used instead to keep the pupil moving and prevent synechiae.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are recognised complications of anterior uveitis EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Cataract, secondary glaucoma (from synechiae/trabecular blockage), and iris atrophy (as in Fuchs' heterochromic uveitis) are recognised complications of anterior uveitis. Retinal detachment is not a typical direct complication of anterior chamber inflammation.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following organisms/causes is classically associated with both keratitis and uveitis in the same patient?
allQuestions.explanation: HSV can cause both dendritic keratitis and an associated anterior uveitis/iridocyclitis as part of the same recurrent infection, reflecting shared viral involvement of the anterior segment.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is one of the earliest features of anterior uveitis on slit-lamp examination?
allQuestions.explanation: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber are the direct, earliest sign of active inflammation, appearing before keratic precipitates, synechiae, or hypopyon develop with more established or severe disease.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following does NOT occur in uveitis?
options: Posterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the lens and bind down the pupil
Anterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the trabecular meshwork or cornea, occluding the drainage angle
originalOptions: Posterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the lens and bind down the pupil
Anterior synechiae, where the iris may adhere to the trabecular meshwork or cornea, occluding the drainage angle
allQuestions.explanation: Hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber, classically from trauma, not a feature of uveitis. Hypopyon (white cells), synechiae, and raised IOP (from synechiae/inflammatory debris blocking outflow) are all recognised uveitis findings.

allQuestions.text: A 23-year-old Caucasian man with acutely painful red eye, photophobia, and morning-stiffness lower back pain. Which of the following statements is FALSE? [img: caucasianmananterioruveitis.png ]
options: The diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
Keratic precipitates and hypopyon are expected findings
The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
Treatment includes topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics
originalOptions: The diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
Keratic precipitates and hypopyon are expected findings
The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
Treatment includes topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The differential diagnosis includes intermediate uveitis
allQuestions.explanation: This presentation — acute pain, photophobia, and a red eye — is classic for anterior uveitis, not intermediate uveitis, which typically presents with painless floaters and vitritis rather than an acutely painful red eye.

allQuestions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with a yellowish retinal lesion and necrosis. The likely diagnosis is:
allQuestions.explanation: CMV retinitis presents as a necrotising retinitis with haemorrhage (classically described as a "pizza-pie" fundus), typically in significantly immunosuppressed patients, and needs systemic antiviral treatment.

allQuestions.text: A 56-year-old lady with known sarcoidosis on systemic prednisolone presents with photophobia, redness, and blurred vision, with no previous eye history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a classic cause of granulomatous uveitis, and the triad of photophobia, redness, and blurred vision fits anterior uveitis rather than the milder discomfort of episcleritis, the external picture of bacterial conjunctivitis, or a traumatic corneal abrasion.

allQuestions.text: In anterior uveitis, the pupil is generally:
allQuestions.explanation: Inflammation causes miosis, and posterior synechiae (iris adhering to the anterior lens capsule) produce an irregular, poorly dilating pupil — a hallmark finding in anterior uveitis, distinct from the fixed, mid-dilated pupil of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

allQuestions.text: A case of anterior uveitis is shown, with ciliary (limbal) injection and keratic precipitates visible on the corneal endothelium. This presentation is most consistent with an underlying joint disease. The full findings, differential diagnoses, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: anterioruveitis3images.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Findings — ciliary (limbal) injection and keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium. Differential diagnoses — ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile chronic arthritis, reactive arthritis (Reiter's disease). Treatment — topical corticosteroids plus mydriatics/cycloplegics (e.g., cyclopentolate or atropine drops).

allQuestions.text: A 23-year-old Caucasian man presents with an acutely painful, red right eye and marked photophobia. History reveals lower back pain for several months, with morning stiffness. The diagnosis, key findings, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: caucasianmananterioruveitis.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Diagnosis — acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27-related). Key findings — keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and hypopyon (a pus layer in the anterior chamber). Treatment — topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics/mydriatics.

allQuestions.text: A 23-year-old man with backache and oral ulcers is referred with right eye pain and photophobia, and a history of previous mild blurred vision episodes. The pathological findings, differential diagnoses, and treatment for this case will be provided in the explanation. [img: hypopyon23keraticprecipitates.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Findings — hypopyon (accumulation of white cells in the anterior chamber inferiorly) and keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium, indicating acute anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis). Differential diagnoses — Behçet's disease (most likely, given oral ulcers and young age), ankylosing spondylitis (associated with backache and HLA-B27), inflammatory bowel disease-associated uveitis / reactive arthritis / sarcoidosis. Treatments — topical or systemic corticosteroids, and topical cycloplegics/mydriatics (e.g., atropine).

allQuestions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with a painful red eye and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination shows keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and posterior synechiae, with the iris adherent to the anterior lens capsule producing an irregular pupil. Which of the following statements about this presentation is FALSE?
options: Keratic precipitates are deposits of inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium
Posterior synechiae is adhesion of the iris to the anterior lens capsule
This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
Cycloplegics help prevent further synechiae formation
originalOptions: Keratic precipitates are deposits of inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium
Posterior synechiae is adhesion of the iris to the anterior lens capsule
This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
Cycloplegics help prevent further synechiae formation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: This presentation is consistent with intermediate uveitis
allQuestions.explanation: Keratic precipitates and posterior synechiae are findings of anterior uveitis, not intermediate uveitis, which instead presents with vitritis and floaters without these anterior segment signs.

allQuestions.text: Arrange the five histological layers of the cornea in correct anterior-to-posterior order:
options: Epithelium → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Endothelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Epithelium
Epithelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Endothelium
Bowman's layer → Epithelium → Stroma → Endothelium → Descemet's membrane
originalOptions: Epithelium → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
Endothelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Epithelium
Epithelium → Descemet's membrane → Stroma → Bowman's layer → Endothelium
Bowman's layer → Epithelium → Stroma → Endothelium → Descemet's membrane
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Epithelium → Bowman's layer → Stroma → Descemet's membrane → Endothelium
allQuestions.explanation: The correct anterior-to-posterior sequence is epithelium (regenerates fast) → Bowman's layer (does not regenerate) → stroma (~90% of thickness) → Descemet's membrane (basement membrane) → endothelium (pump layer, does not regenerate).

allQuestions.text: The main route of aqueous humour outflow, accounting for approximately 90–96% of drainage, is:
options: The uveoscleral pathway through the ciliary body face
The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
originalOptions: The uveoscleral pathway through the ciliary body face
The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal
allQuestions.explanation: Aqueous drains conventionally through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal and then into episcleral veins, accounting for the large majority of outflow; the uveoscleral route handles only about 4–10%. This conventional pathway is the main pharmacological target in glaucoma treatment.

allQuestions.text: Which structure is responsible for producing the outer lipid layer of the tear film, and what is its main function?
options: Lacrimal gland; provides 90% of tear thickness
Goblet cells; wets the hydrophobic corneal epithelium
Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
Accessory lacrimal glands; delivers antibacterial proteins
originalOptions: Lacrimal gland; provides 90% of tear thickness
Goblet cells; wets the hydrophobic corneal epithelium
Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
Accessory lacrimal glands; delivers antibacterial proteins
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Meibomian glands; retards evaporation of the aqueous layer
allQuestions.explanation: The meibomian glands, located within the tarsal plates, secrete the outer lipid layer whose main job is to slow evaporation of the underlying aqueous layer. Dysfunction of these glands is a major cause of evaporative dry eye.

allQuestions.text: Contraction of which iris muscle produces mydriasis, and via which autonomic pathway?
allQuestions.explanation: The dilator pupillae consists of radial fibres under sympathetic control, producing mydriasis, whereas the sphincter pupillae is circular and parasympathetically innervated (CN III), producing miosis.

allQuestions.text: Cones, responsible for colour vision and fine visual acuity, are exclusively found at which retinal location?
allQuestions.explanation: Cones are concentrated at the macula and are exclusively present at its centre, the fovea centralis, which is the point of sharpest vision. Rods, by contrast, are far more numerous but absent from the very centre of the fovea, mediating dim-light and peripheral vision instead.

allQuestions.text: The optic disc corresponds to the physiological blind spot because:
options: It is the thinnest part of the retina
It is where the vitreous attaches most firmly
originalOptions: It is the thinnest part of the retina
It is where the vitreous attaches most firmly
allQuestions.explanation: The optic disc is where retinal ganglion cell axons converge and exit the eye as the optic nerve; since it contains no photoreceptors, it corresponds to the physiological blind spot. This is distinct from the fovea, which has the highest photoreceptor density.

allQuestions.text: The vitreous body is firmly attached at all of the following sites EXCEPT:
options: The vitreous base, just behind the ora serrata
None of the above — all are correct attachment sites
originalOptions: The vitreous base, just behind the ora serrata
None of the above — all are correct attachment sites
allQuestions.explanation: The vitreous body is attached to the vitreous base (peripheral retina/pars plana), the optic disc margin, and the macula. While its attachment to the macula and retinal vessels is relatively less firm than at the base or disc, it remains a critical attachment site. These locations are clinically significant because they experience traction and pulling when the vitreous shrinks with age. The lens equator is not a vitreous attachment site.

allQuestions.text: The conjunctiva contains goblet cells whose function is to:
options: Produce the outer lipid layer of the tear film
Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
Provide sensory innervation to the ocular surface
originalOptions: Produce the outer lipid layer of the tear film
Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
Provide sensory innervation to the ocular surface
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Secrete the mucin layer of the tear film
allQuestions.explanation: Goblet cells within the conjunctiva secrete mucin, which allows the aqueous tear layer to wet the otherwise hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly. The conjunctiva itself has bulbar and palpebral parts meeting at the fornices.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the correct pairing of a uveal tract structure with its principal role?
options: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
originalOptions: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Choroid — supplies the outer retina via the choriocapillaris
allQuestions.explanation: The choroid is the posterior, vascular part of the uveal tract, and its capillary layer (the choriocapillaris) supplies the outer retina, including the photoreceptors. New vessel growth from the choroid through Bruch's membrane is also the underlying mechanism of wet age-related macular degeneration.

allQuestions.text: Select all correct statements regarding the three concentric layers of the globe:
options: The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera
The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid
The inner neural coat is the retina
The lens forms part of the outer fibrous coat
The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
originalOptions: The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera
The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid
The inner neural coat is the retina
The lens forms part of the outer fibrous coat
The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera / B) The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid / C) The inner neural coat is the retina / E) The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A) The outer fibrous coat is composed of the cornea and sclera / B) The middle vascular coat (uveal tract) includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid / C) The inner neural coat is the retina / E) The globe wall is composed of these three concentric layers
allQuestions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are all true — the globe wall consists of an outer fibrous coat (cornea + sclera), a middle vascular coat (uveal tract: iris + ciliary body + choroid), and an inner neural coat (retina). D is false because the lens is one of the three transparent refracting media inside the globe (with aqueous humour and vitreous), not part of the wall itself.

questions.text: Regarding urological imaging studies, what is the most important risk of exposure to ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation from CT and fluoroscopic urological studies carries a cumulative risk of carcinogenesis, making malignancy induction the most clinically significant long-term hazard. Skin irritation and cataracts require far higher cumulative doses to manifest. ## All of the following are true about kidney anatomy, EXCEPT: A) An oval intraperitoneal organ B) Left kidney has a longer renal vein C) Right kidney is smaller than the left kidney D) Kidneys are bean-shaped structures E) Kidneys are bilateral structures Correct Answer: A) An oval intraperitoneal organ Explanation: Kidneys are retroperitoneal, bean-shaped structures, not intraperitoneal. The right kidney sits lower and is often described as slightly smaller, while the left renal vein is longer as it crosses the aorta to reach the IVC.

questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE about kidney anatomy?
options: Kidneys lie posterior in the abdomen
originalOptions: Kidneys lie posterior in the abdomen
questions.explanation: Kidneys lie retroperitoneally against the posterior abdominal wall, not within the peritoneal cavity. All other listed features (bilateral, bean-shaped, posterior location) accurately describe renal anatomy.

questions.text: The correct order of the division of the intrarenal branches of the renal artery is:
questions.explanation: The renal artery branches sequentially from segmental arteries into interlobar arteries running between pyramids, then arcuate arteries arching at the corticomedullary junction, and finally interlobular arteries ascending into the cortex.

questions.text: The only segment of the urethra that does NOT have transitional epithelium is the:
questions.explanation: The fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, distinguishing it from the transitional epithelium lining the more proximal urethral segments listed as options. Another way to phrase the question: Which segment is lined by stratified squamous epithelium? Ans: E.

questions.text: Ultrasound has many advantages which include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: It is safe and does not use ionizing radiation
It requires little or no pre-procedural preparation
It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
It can be safely performed in pregnant women
It is not affected by renal function
originalOptions: It is safe and does not use ionizing radiation
It requires little or no pre-procedural preparation
It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
It can be safely performed in pregnant women
It is not affected by renal function
questions.correctAnswer: C) It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
questions.correctAnswerText: It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is limited in differentiating pseudotumors from true renal lesions; CT or MRI are superior for this characterization. Its safety, minimal preparation, and independence from renal function are genuine advantages.

questions.text: Which of the following is associated with suprapubic pain?
questions.explanation: Bladder pathology such as cystitis or overdistension classically produces suprapubic discomfort, whereas renal colic and ureteric stones typically cause flank pain radiating to the groin.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding physical examination?
options: The testes in men should be the same size
The normal prostate is the size of a walnut
A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
It is best to examine a man's genitalia in a warm room
originalOptions: The testes in men should be the same size
The normal prostate is the size of a walnut
A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
It is best to examine a man's genitalia in a warm room
questions.correctAnswer: D) A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
questions.correctAnswerText: A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
questions.explanation: A "bag of worms" texture describes a varicocele, not a hydrocele; a hydrocele is a smooth, fluid-filled swelling that transilluminates. A warm room helps relax the cremasteric reflex for accurate examination.

questions.text: All the following can cause a DECREASE in specific gravity of urine EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dehydration concentrates the urine, raising specific gravity, whereas increased fluid intake, diuretics, and impaired concentrating ability all dilute urine and lower specific gravity.

questions.text: Which of the following are used in the calculation of plasma osmolarity?
questions.explanation: Plasma osmolarity is estimated as 2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, incorporating sodium as the main osmotic contributor along with glucose and urea.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about renal pain?
options: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
originalOptions: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
questions.explanation: Renal pain arises from capsular distension, with inflammatory pain being steady while obstructive pain fluctuates; it can also mimic intraperitoneal pathology, though patients with renal pain classically prefer to move (rolling sign) unlike those with peritoneal pain.

questions.text: Choose the WRONG statement about kidney anatomy:
options: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
Left kidney is higher than the right
Right kidney extends from 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
Left kidney extends from 12th thoracic to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
The right kidney is displaced inferiorly by the liver
originalOptions: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
Left kidney is higher than the right
Right kidney extends from 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
Left kidney extends from 12th thoracic to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
The right kidney is displaced inferiorly by the liver
questions.correctAnswer: A) Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
questions.correctAnswerText: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
questions.explanation: The right kidney actually lies 1-2 cm lower than the left due to the liver's position above it, making the left kidney the higher of the two.

questions.text: Choose the WRONG statement:
options: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
Obstruction causes colicky pain and inflammation causes steady pain
Renal colic fluctuates in intensity as the kidney attempts to relieve obstruction
Steady inflammatory pain reflects capsular distension without peristaltic surges
Obstructive pain fluctuates due to ureteral peristalsis against the blockage
originalOptions: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
Obstruction causes colicky pain and inflammation causes steady pain
Renal colic fluctuates in intensity as the kidney attempts to relieve obstruction
Steady inflammatory pain reflects capsular distension without peristaltic surges
Obstructive pain fluctuates due to ureteral peristalsis against the blockage
questions.correctAnswer: A) Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
questions.correctAnswerText: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
questions.explanation: This reverses the actual pattern: inflammatory renal pain is steady, while obstructive pain fluctuates in intensity as the ureter undergoes hyperperistalsis to overcome the blockage.

questions.text: Radiographically, the ureter is divided into how many parts?
questions.explanation: The ureter is anatomically and radiologically divided into upper, middle (over the sacrum), and lower segments, corresponding to abdominal, pelvic, and intramural portions.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs does NOT cause renal failure?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used for bladder outlet obstruction and lacks nephrotoxic potential, unlike ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, and NSAIDs, which can impair renal perfusion or cause direct tubular injury.

questions.text: Which imaging modality is safest for a patient in renal failure?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound requires no contrast or radiation exposure and is unaffected by renal function, making it the safest imaging choice in renal impairment, unlike iodinated or gadolinium-based contrast studies which risk nephrotoxicity or nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

questions.text: Renal pain classically radiates to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain radiates from the flank toward the groin and may be referred to the testis due to shared T11-T12 innervation, distinguishing it from intraperitoneal pain, which classically radiates to the shoulder.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the male urethra from proximal to distal?
questions.explanation: The male urethra begins at the bladder neck, passing through the prostatic segment, then the membranous urethra at the external sphincter, followed by the bulbar and pendulous penile urethra ending at the fossa navicularis.

questions.text: A patient presents with flank pain. Which feature would favor a urological (renal) rather than an intraperitoneal cause?
options: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
originalOptions: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
